This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Is there an infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ such that\[\lvert x_{n+1}-x_n\rvert \ll 1?\]
#952: [Er77c][Er80,p.114]
number theory
The Gaussian moat problem. This is not actually a problem of Erdős, but has been erroneously attributed to him in the past. In [Er77c] Erdős recalls: 'The conjecture was told me by Motzkin at the Pasadena number theory meeting 1963 November and it was apparently raised by Basil Gordon and Motzkin. I naturally liked it very much and told it right away to many people, naturally attributing it to Motzkin, but this was later forgotten. Thus the problem is returned to its rightful owners.'
In [Er80] Erdős writes 'the answer is almost certainly negative'.

 Wikipedia says "Computational searches have shown that the origin is separated from infinity by a moat of width 6" and links to this reference: Tsuchimura, Nobuyuki (2005), "Computational results for Gaussian moat problem", IEICE Transactions on Fundamentals of Electronics, Communications and Computer Sciences, 88 (5): 1267–1273, Bibcode:2005IEITF..88.1267T, doi:10.1093/ietfec/e88-a.5.1267.
I really enjoyed the article. In the end, the author includes some simple but nice plots. Their computational results are very consistent with a random model of Gaussian primes, for which the answer is "no, such a bounded infinite sequence does not exist".

 There is an $M$ and a sequence of Gaussian primes $\{\gamma_j\}_{1^\infty}$, such that $|\gamma_1| < M$, $|\gamma_j - \gamma_{j-1}| < M$ and $\lim |\gamma_j| = \infty$.
J. H. Jordan and J. R. Rabung has showed that if the conjecture is true, then $M \geq 4$, in A Conjecture of Paul Erdős Concerning Gaussian Primes(1970).
Thanks To Vjeko for pointing the mistakes out!

 As far as I can see, Jordan and Rabung did not establish the conjecture (I mean the Gaussian moat problem), but rather 
''report that if the conjecture is true then $M\geq4$''.
They also performed a computer search that led them to believe that the conjecture *might* be true.
Last time I checked the literature, it seemed that the claim was still open.

 I might not have been reading your post carefully either, because now I see that you mention some alternative conjecture, and that it does not make sense. The condition $|\gamma_j|<M$ is in a contradiction with $\lim|\gamma_j|=\infty$. So this was just a typo somewhere! What Jordan and Ranburg actually write is $|\gamma_1|<M$, in which case this is the original "Gaussian moat problem". There was no alternative version of the conjecture at all.
